statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama came that very day from Vrindavan with Akrura, who drove them in his chariot and went ahead to the palace, leaving the brothers to walk the city.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.82: Akrura set out with Krishna and Sankarshana, reached Mathura before evening, then went to Kamsa leaving the two to visit the highways; consistent with Bhagavata 10.41 chain.

statements.claim: They walked through Mathura like two elephants loosed from their posts.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.82: 'went on visiting all the high-ways like two elephants let free from their posts'.

statements.claim: They met the king's washerman carrying the king's own dyed cloth, gathered from many countries.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.82: 'I dye, as he desires, all the clothes of the king Kansa which he gets from various countries'; Vishnu Purana 5.19: washerman was Kamsa's servant.

statements.claim: Krishna asked the washerman for clothes that would suit the two of them.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.41.32: 'dehy āvayoḥ samucitāny aṅga vāsāṃsi'.

statements.claim: The washerman refused and abused them, calling them forest rangers born among the deer, stupid, of inferior understanding, and warning them to drop the request if they valued their lives.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.41.33-35; Harivamsha 1.82: 'born in a forest you have grown up with the deer... stupid and of inferior intellect... Perhaps giving up all hopes of your life you have come here'.

statements.claim: Destiny was against that washerman.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.82: 'Destiny was against that stupid washer-man of feeble understanding'.

statements.claim: Krishna, his anger rising, struck him a single blow of his open hand across the head, and the man fell and lay still.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.41.36 (struck off his head with his hand); Harivamsha 1.82: struck him on the head with his fist, 'with his head sundered he fell down lifeless on earth'.

statements.claim: The washerman's attendants dropped their bundles of dyed cloth and ran.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.41.37: 'tasyānujīvinaḥ sarve vāsaḥ-kośān visṛjya'.

statements.claim: The brothers chose garments for themselves and gave the rest away to the cowherds who had come from Vrindavan.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.41.38 (Krishna and Sankarshana wore garments dear to themselves); pack summary: 'took the garments and distributed them to the cowherds'.

statements.claim: The dye sat freshly on the cloth, red and yellow and deep blue.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric colour detail; pack confirms the cloth was dyed in many colours (Harivamsha 1.82).

notes: All factual claims supported by Bhagavata 10.41.31-38 / Harivamsha 1.82 / Vishnu Purana 5.19. Story follows Bhagavata variant (attendants flee; garments distributed to cowherds), which the pack endorses.

statements.claim: In a hall in Mathura stood a great bow, the most guarded thing in the city, standing on a stand, worshipped and decked with offerings, ringed by armed men.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.15: 'puruṣair bahubhir guptam arcitaṃ paramarddhimat' (guarded by many men, worshipped, most splendid).

statements.claim: The bow was the centrepiece of the festival the king was preparing.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.82 refers to the 'bow-sacrifice' Krishna came to witness; festival context of the arc.

statements.claim: Krishna asked the townspeople where the famous bow was kept.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.14: 'tataḥ paurān pṛcchamāno dhanuṣaḥ sthānam acyutaḥ'.

statements.claim: The guards forbade him, but he took the great bow in his left hand, lifted it easily, and strung it in a single moment.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.16: 'kareṇa vāmena sa-līlam uddhṛtaṃ sajyaṃ ca kṛtvā nimiṣeṇa paśyatām'; pack excerpt: seized it though the guards forbade him.

statements.claim: He bent it and it snapped in two at the middle like a stalk of sugarcane, and the sound filled the sky, the earth and every direction, so that all Mathura heard it.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.16-17 (sugarcane simile; 'śabdaḥ khaṃ rodasī diśaḥ'); Vishnu Purana 5.20: 'all Mathurá resounded with the noise'.

statements.claim: The guards and their followers came at them, and Krishna and Balarama struck down the whole force Kamsa had sent, using the two broken halves of the bow.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.18-20: 'tad-rakṣiṇaḥ sānucaraṃ kupitā ātatāyinaḥ... balaṃ ca kaṃsa-prahitaṃ hatvā'.

statements.claim: The townspeople marvelled, and the sun was going down as they walked out into the city.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.21-22 (townsfolk saw the wonderful valour; 'ādityo 'stam upeyivān').

statements.claim: No archer's hand had drawn the bow in living memory.
statements.evidence: Rhetorical framing of the bow's sacred, unused status; not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: By nightfall there was not a household that had not heard the tale told twice.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric hyperbole following 10.42.21 (townspeople witnessed and spoke of the feat).

notes: All key events match Bhagavata 10.42.13-22 (left-hand lift, stringing, sugarcane snap, noise filling Mathura, guards struck down with the two halves).

statements.claim: The news reached Kamsa that the great bow was broken and the men he had set to guard it were dead.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.25: 'kaṃsas tu dhanuṣo bhaṅgaṃ rakṣiṇāṃ sva-balasya ca'.

statements.claim: He had known the two young men were coming for years and watched for them fearfully.
statements.evidence: Canonical arc background (Kamsa's long-standing fear of the prophecy, established in earlier corpus stories); consistent with the pack, not contradicted.

statements.claim: That night Kamsa did not sleep; fear kept him awake.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.26: 'dīrgha-prajāgaro bhīto durnimittāni durmatiḥ' (long wakefulness, terrified, evil omens).

statements.claim: He looked into a mirror and could not see his own head in the reflection, though his face should have been there.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.27: 'adarśanaṃ sva-śirasaḥ pratirūpe ca saty api'.

statements.claim: He looked at his shadow and saw a hole running through it, and strained to hear his own breathing and heard nothing.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.28: 'chidra-pratītiś chāyāyāṃ prāṇa-ghoṣānupaśrutiḥ'.

statements.claim: In dreams he embraced a corpse and rode an ass through the night, and a heaviness and dejection settled over everything.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.29: 'svapne preta-pariṣvaṅgaḥ khara-yānaṃ viṣādanam'.

statements.claim: By morning he had seen his own death in every sign; the omens all said the same thing.
statements.evidence: Pack summary: omens and dreams 'all foretelling his death'; Bhagavata 10.42.30 ('anyāni cetthaṃ-bhūtāni svapna-jāgaritāni ca').

notes: All omens map directly to Bhagavata 10.42.23-30 verses. The 'known for years' line reflects the arc's established prophecy background (previous stories), not the pack passage, but is consistent and uncontradicted.

statements.claim: When the night ended and the sun rose out of the waters, Kamsa gave his order: let the wrestling begin.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.31-32: 'vyuṣṭāyāṃ niśi... sūrye cādbhyaḥ samutthite... tūrya-bheryaś ca jaghnire'.

statements.claim: The arena was prepared with drums and kettledrums sounding, the noise reaching every corner of Mathura.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.32: 'ānarcuḥ puruṣā raṅgaṃ tūrya-bheryaś ca jaghnire'.

statements.claim: Citizens and country folk poured in, brahmins and kshatriyas at their head, until the stands were full.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.33: 'teṣu paurā jānapadā brahma-kṣatra-purogamāḥ'.

statements.claim: Kamsa climbed to the royal dais with his ministers around him.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.34: 'kaṃsaḥ parivṛto 'mātyai rāja-mañca upāviśat'.

statements.claim: The wrestlers took their places: Chanura, Mushtika, Kuta, Shala and Toshala.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.36: 'cāṇūro muṣṭikaḥ kūtaḥ śalas tośala eva ca'.

statements.claim: Summoned by the Bhoja king, Nanda and the cowherds arrived bearing their offerings.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.42.37: 'nanda-gopādayo gopā bhoja-rāja-samāhutāḥ'; pack excerpt: 'arrived with their offerings'.

statements.claim: Ropes were drawn around the wrestling ground.
statements.evidence: Plausible arena detail; not explicitly in the pack verses, no contradiction.

notes: Matches Bhagavata 10.42.31-37 point by point, including the 'sun risen from the waters' detail and the full wrestler list.

statements.claim: At the gate of the wrestling arena stood the elephant Kuvalayapida; Kamsa had ordered 'let it wait at the gate'.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.1 ('raṅga-dvāraṃ samāsādya tasmin nāgam avasthitam'); Harivamsha 1.84: 'Having ordered "Let the elephant Kuvalyapida wait at the gate"'.

statements.claim: The arena rose on octagonal pillars painted in many colours, hung with festoons of flowers and the banners of every guild, with gold and gems and seats and couches; Kamsa's pavilion shone like a mountain of snow.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.84 (2-15): octagonal painted pillars, festoons of flowers, banners of the crafts, gold and gems, cushioned seats; Kamsa's pavilion 'like mount Meru in radiance', the king shining 'like the moon... on the white summit of the white mountain'.

statements.claim: The king entered in white with white chowries waving, took his throne, and the citizens shouted his praises; the wrestlers, loose-garmented, took the ground on three sides.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.84 (18-20): two white chowries, white raiment and turban, citizens' shouts of victory, wrestlers with loose garments on three sides.

statements.claim: Krishna tied back his garments and gathered his curling hair before approaching.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.2: 'baddhvā parikaraṃ śauriḥ samuhya kuṭilālakān'.

statements.claim: He told the elephant's keeper to stand aside and make way; the keeper, stung, goaded the beast, which came forward with trunk folded to crush them.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.3-4; Harivamsha 1.84: 'that wicked elephant, folding up its trunk, attempted to destroy Rama and Krishna'.

statements.claim: Krishna slipped beneath it, took hold of its tail, and dragged it back the length of twenty-five bows; he moved between its tusks and under its legs like the wind troubling the sea.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.7-8 ('pucche pragṛhyāti-balaṃ dhanuṣaḥ pañca-viṃśatim'; 'savya-dakṣiṇato'); Harivamsha 1.84: 'agitated him as does wind the ocean'.

statements.claim: He roared like a lion, slapped his arms, and let the elephant's trunk come against his chest; the enraged beast, seeing only by smell, could not find him.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.5-6 ('ghrāṇa-dṛṣṭiḥ'); Harivamsha 1.84 (26-27): roaring like a lion, slapping arms, taking the trunk on his breast.

statements.claim: He sported with the elephant in a childlike way, smiling, and said Kamsa, in trying to kill him through the elephant, was only hurrying himself to the abode of Yama.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.10-11 ('sa dhāvan kṛīdayā'); Harivamsha 1.84 (24-25): 'he is eager to repair to the abode of Yama'; 'sporting with that elephant under the pretext of a childish freak'.

statements.claim: On the second charge he pressed it down and set his foot on it like a lion settling its prey, tore out both tusks with his two hands and beat it with them; it discharged must like a cloud in the rains and lay still, blood dark at its temples.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.12-14; Harivamsha 1.84 (31-35): foot on the lower lip, uprooting the tusks with both hands, must discharged 'like a cloud in the rains', blood from the temples.

statements.claim: Its keepers fell with it.
statements.evidence: Pack summary of Bhagavata 10.43.1-15: 'slew the beast and its keepers'.

statements.claim: Krishna took up one of the tusks, and he and Balarama, surrounded by the cowherds, entered the arena covered with the elephant's blood and must.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.14-15 ('danta-pāṇiḥ samāviśat'; 'vṛtau gopaiḥ katipayair baladeva-janārdanau'); Harivamsha 1.85 and Vishnu Purana 5.20: 'covered with must and blood' entered the arena.

statements.claim: Kamsa watched from his high seat as the two came forward.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.84: the king seated on his throne in the arena; consistent with the narrative.

notes: Follows the Bhagavata variant (Krishna alone slays the elephant), as the tradition_note states; all details including the 25-bow drag and tusk removal are verse-backed.

statements.claim: Krishna walked into the arena holding the elephant's tusk, Balarama at his side, the two great-armed, in bright garments, garlands and ornaments.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.14, 17-18: tusk in hand ('danta-pāṇiḥ'); 'mahā-bhujau vicitra-veṣābharaṇa-srag-ambarau'.

statements.claim: The galleries were full — townsmen and countrymen, kings and commoners, wrestlers and merchants, women at the screened windows — and the people drank the two in with their eyes and as if with their tongues.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.19-20 ('nāgara-rāṣṭrakā nṛpa'; 'pibanta iva cakṣurbhyāṃ lihanta iva jihvayā'); Harivamsha 1.84: women viewing through 'delicate jealousies' (screened windows).

statements.claim: Each person saw him according to his own heart: a thunderbolt to the wrestlers, best of men to ordinary men, embodied love to the women, a kinsman to the cowherds, a chastiser to the wicked among the kings, the highest truth to the ignorant, the goal of the yogis, the supreme deity of the Vrishnis, a child to his parents, and death to the lord of the Bhojas, Kamsa.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.16: 'mallānām aśanir nṛṇāṃ nara-varaḥ strīṇāṃ smaro mūrtimān / gopānāṃ sva-jano 'satāṃ kṣiti-bhujāṃ śāstā sva-pitroḥ śiśuḥ / mṛtyur bhoja-pater virāḍ aviduṣāṃ tattvaṃ paraṃ yogināṃ vṛṣṇīnāṃ para-devatā'.

statements.claim: The people recounted his deeds: born to Devaki and carried to Gokula; the end of Putana and the whirlwind demon; saving the cows and cowherds from the forest fire; holding up a great hill on one hand for seven days; the gopis' delight in his smiling glance; the fame of the Yadu line; and the elder brother, the glorious lotus-eyed Rama.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.23-29: 'eṣa vai kila devakyāṃ jāto nītaś ca gokulam / pūtanānena nītāntaṃ cakravātaś ca dānavaḥ / gāvaḥ sa-pālā etena dāvāgneḥ parimocitāḥ / saptāham eka-hastena dhṛto 'dri-pravaro 'munā / gopyo 'sya nitya-mudita-hasita-prekṣaṇaṃ mukham / vadanty anena vaṃśo 'yaṃ yadoḥ su-bahu-viśrutaḥ / ayaṃ cāsyāgrajaḥ śrīmān rāmaḥ kamala-locanaḥ'.

statements.claim: The city had come to watch them die, and for a moment forgot it.
statements.evidence: Framing of the crowd's wonder; consistent with the pack's theme (delight and rejoicing before the fight).

notes: The multi-perspective description and the entire remembered-deeds catalogue map directly onto Bhagavata 10.43.16-30.

statements.claim: Chanura, a wrestler and Kamsa's champion, walked into the centre of the arena and addressed the two brothers, calling them 'Son of Nanda' and 'Rama', saying heroes are counted as such, that those who please the king find their welfare, that the cowherds are always cheerful, and proposing that both they and he do what pleases the king.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.31-34: 'he nanda-sūno he rāma bhavantau vīra-sammatau / priyaṃ rājñaḥ prakurvatyaḥ śreyo vindanti vai prajāḥ / nityaṃ pramuditā gopā... / tasmād rājñaḥ priyaṃ yūyaṃ vayaṃ ca karavāma he'.

statements.claim: Krishna's reply was fitted to the time and place: 'We are subjects of this lord of the Bhojas, but we are forest-dwellers; we are boys and will play with those of equal strength, as is proper.'
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.35-37: 'deśa-kālocitaṃ vacaḥ / prajā bhoja-pater asya vayaṃ cāpi vane-carāḥ / bālā vayaṃ tulya-balaiḥ krīḍiṣyāmo yathocitam'.

statements.claim: Chanura insisted the fight must go forward and that there was no injustice in it, saying he would meet Krishna and Mushtika would face Balarama.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.43.38-39 ('tasmād bhavadbhyāṃ balibhir yoddhavyaṃ nānayo 'tra vai'); pack summary: 'Chanura urged, "Fight me, and let Mushtika fight Balarama"'.

statements.claim: Chanura was a wrestler who had made his name breaking the men he was set against.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.85: Chanura 'has put a stigma on the ways of wrestlers by destroying many of them after their discomfiture'.

statements.claim: High above the ring Kamsa watched from his throne and said nothing, letting his champion press the match.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric; consistent with Kamsa seated on the royal dais (10.42.34) and the events' intent. Not explicitly stated in 10.43.30-39.

notes: The dialogue closely tracks Bhagavata 10.43.30-39; the Mushtika-pairing detail is endorsed by the pack summary.

statements.claim: After Kamsa lay dead and the wrestlers had fallen, his eight younger brothers — Kanka, Nyagrodha and the rest — came rushing at Krishna in fury.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.44.39: 'tasyānujā bhrātaro 'ṣṭau kaṅka-nyagrodhakādayaḥ'; pack summary: 'rushed at Krishna in fury'.

statements.claim: Balarama, the elder, son of Rohini, stepped between them and Krishna and slew all eight with his club, like a lion moving through cattle.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.44.40: 'tathāti-rabhasāṃs tāṃs tu saṃyattān rohiṇī-sutaḥ'; pack summary: 'Balarama slew them all with his club, like a lion among cattle'.

statements.claim: He took the proudest of them in his two hands and felled him as easily as the rest.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.85: 'Holding powerfully by his hands the proud brother of Kansa, by name Urgita, the virtuous-souled Baladeva killed him'.

statements.claim: The elephant's tusk was still in Krishna's hand when the brothers charged.
statements.evidence: Consistent with Bhagavata 10.43.14 (tusk in hand at the arena entrance) and 10.44 sequence; uncontradicted.

statements.claim: The house of Kamsa had spent years sending its killers after a child.
statements.evidence: Canonical arc background (Kamsa's attempts on the infant Krishna, prior stories); consistent with the pack, uncontradicted.

statements.claim: The verses give the brothers only a line of names and the single motion of their charge; one club, eight men, and then silence.
statements.evidence: Rhetorical compression of Bhagavata 10.44.39-40, which indeed devotes only two verses to the episode.

notes: Follows the Bhagavata (parents' greeting kept separate, per tradition_note); the Urgita detail from Harivamsha is used only where it fits ('the proudest of them').
